Transition theory emphasizes the resources individuals bring to their transitions.  Turning points theory emphasizes the impact of transitions on individuals. RNA polymerase copies genetic information from non coding DNA strand as the coding strand is being transcribed into mRNA. The leading strand and protein strand are parts of the DNA molecules. The TATA box is a sequence of nucleotides that occurs at the start site of transcription. It is not a part of the RNA molecule and therefore cannot be copied from.  This question tests the understanding of how DNA is transcribed to RNA and what happens during this process. This question also tests the knowledge of the different components of DNA and RNA. Students should know that RNA polymerase copies genetic information from the non coding DNA strand and they will need to understand why it is the non coding strand since the coding strand is involved in the transcription process. They should know the difference between the coding and non coding strands and they should know that RNA polymerase is located on the non coding strand so it makes sense that the non coding strand would be the one which contains the genetic information. The role of the TATA box is to mark the start site for transcription. It is not a part of the RNA molecule so it cannot be copied from. If students are confused with the differences between the DNA and RNA strands or if they don't understand the functions of the TATA box then they may select answers based on these confusions. Sensitivity - The proportion of persons with disease who are correctly identified by a screening test as having the disease. This refers to the proportion of patients with a positive screening test who have the condition. For example, if a patient has a positive screening test for a particular type of cancer, what proportion of those patients will actually have the cancer? Negative predictive value - The proportion of persons without disease who are correctly identified by a screening test as not having the disease This refers to the proportion of patients with a negative screening test who do not have the condition. For example, if a patient has a negative screening test for a particular type of cancer, what proportion of those patients do not have the cancer? Prevalence - Rate at which new cases occur in a population during a specified period This is the proportion of the population who have a certain disease at a specific point in time. It does not tell you how likely it is that an individual member of the population will develop the disease. For example, if there are 100 people in a village and 5 of them have heart failure, then the prevalence of heart failure in the village is 5%. Incidence - Proportion of a population that are cases during a specified period of time This is similar to prevalence but tells you how likely it is that an individual member of the population will develop the disease over a particular period of time. For example, if there are 100 people in a village and 2 of them developed heart failure last year, then the incidence of heart failure in the village is 2%. Specificity - The number of true negatives out of all the negatives given by the test This is the proportion of patients who received a negative test result who do not have the condition. For example, if a patient has a negative screening test for a particular type of cancer, what proportion of those patients do not have the cancer? Group A streptococci (GAS) is the most common causative agent of rheumatic fever. It is a gram-positive cocci that can cause a wide range of diseases from minor skin infections to severe invasive disease. Symptoms of rheumatic fever include arthritis, fever and polynodular skin rashes. Rheumatic heart disease is a later complication of the condition. The heart valves may be damaged by immunologic mechanisms including collagen deposition and cell proliferation. This results in stenosis or insufficiency of the mitral, tricuspid or aortic valve.  Rheumatic fever may follow an acute streptococcal pharyngitis, scarlet fever or perianal dermatitis. The risk of developing rheumatic fever following GAS infection is highest in children aged 3-10 years. The incidence of rheumatic fever varies between populations but it remains relatively common in areas with poor living conditions and high population density. It is also more prevalent in indigenous communities.  Rheumatic fever cannot be treated with antibiotics as the damage is mediated by the body's own immune response. However, penicillin is given to prevent recurrent episodes of GAS infection which may exacerbate the rheumatic fever.  Symptoms of rheumatic fever are treated with NSAIDs. Corticosteroids may be used in severe cases.  Prevention of rheumatic fever relies on early identification and treatment of streptococcal pharyngitis with antibiotics. Antibiotic prophylaxis is recommended in children who have had recent GAS infection or a family member with rheumatic fever. Sentinel cells are macrophages (including microglial cells), dendritic cells and Langerhan cells. They are found at the entry points of the body, i.e. skin, mucous membranes etc. They have a pattern recognition receptor which recognises viral antigens. When this occurs, they activate the complement system, and release cytokines which attract phagocytes. These phagocytes engulf the virus and travel to the lymph node nearest to the site of entry. There, they encounter naive T-cells and B-cells. The T-cells now undergo clonal expansion, where they proliferate into effector and memory T-cells. The B-cells also undergo clonal expansion, differentiating into plasma cells so they can pump out antibodies, and memory B-cells. The effector T-cells release a cocktail of chemicals, causing apoptosis of infected cells, and inducing the acute stage of inflammation. The virus is trapped within the infected cell, as it cannot exit due to the action of interferons, which prevent the translation of the viral genome. This is called the viral factory, as the virus is being produced but not released. The immune response is now in its effector phase. The adaptive part of the immune response takes about 3 days to kick in, because it takes time for the sentinel cells to detect the pathogen and send signals to the nearest lymph node telling it to produce all those lovely Clones. During this period, the innate response does its best. Macrophages and natural killer cells release granulysin, which forms pores in the plasma membrane of the virus-infected cell, killing it. They also release perforins, which form pores in the mitochondria of the infected cell, leading to rapid cell death. They also use RNAse to destroy the genetic material of the virus. The natural killer cells do not have receptors for antigen, meaning they attack any infected cell they come across. Macrophages only attack cells with appropriate receptors. Carnitine acyltransferase I catalyses the reaction between carnitine and Acyl-CoA, forming acyl-carnitine which can then cross the inner mitochondrial membrane via specialised channels. Once on the other side of the membrane, carnitine acyltransferase II catalyses the reverse reaction, converting acyl-carnitine back into acyl-CoA. This allows acyl-CoA to enter the mitochondria where it can be oxidised by the F0F1 ATPase. The process of crossing the mitochondrial membrane is not very efficient, as only about 30% of the Acyl-CoA molecules are able to cross over. This is because the concentration of carnitine inside the mitochondria is much lower than outside the mitochondria. Since carnitine is also needed for other processes such as muscle metabolism, it cannot be kept at high concentrations within the mitochondria. This means that fatty acid oxidation will never be able to provide enough energy for all our needs, and we must use glucose as well. Anterior cord syndrome is the most common form of spinal cord syndromes and is characterised by bilateral spastic paralysis with a lack of pain and temperature below the level of the lesion. There is also a lack of proprioception and vibration sense. However there is intact 2-point discrimination. This is due to the anterior spino-thalamic tract being affected. Central cord syndrome is less common than anterior cord syndrome. It results from hyperextension trauma of the neck and causes bilateral spastic paralysis with preservation of pain, temperature and 2 point discrimination. However there is loss of proprioception and vibration sense. This is because the central corticospinal tract is damaged in this condition.  Brown-Sèquard syndrome results from a penetrating wound causing damage to the right or left half of the spinal cord. They look at maternal serum levels of: b hCG, inhibin A and unconjugated oestriol. These can be measured between 11-13 and 19-20 weeks. Levels are different in mother with Down’s syndrome baby. If the results of either test is high then the foetus will need to be further assessed by amniocentesis or chorionic villous sampling. These are diagnostic tests which confirm or rule out chromosomal abnormality. Amniocentesis - a sample of amniotic fluid is taken using a long hollow needle inserted through the mothers abdomen.
